:::{#exr-real-coordinate-space-practice}
#### Testing whether a vector with entries $\sqrt{2}$ and $\pi$ lies in $\reals^3$

Entries such as $\sqrt{2}$ and $\pi$ have no exact decimal form,
but they are still [real numbers](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/number-systems.html#def-real-numbers).
Let

$$
\vecf{v} = \sbmat{\sqrt{2} \\ \pi \\ -1}.
$$

Is $\vecf{v}$ in $\reals^3$?

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Hint

@def-real-coordinate-space has two conditions:
the number of entries of the [column vector](#def-column-vector),
and the kind of number in each entry.

:::
